Giant trevally (Caranx ignobilis) is a large apex predator inhabiting tropical and subtropical reef systems across the Indo-Pacific region. Among the largest members of the Carangidae family, this species attains a maximum total length of 170 centimeters [Li = 170 centimeters], making it a formidable hunter capable of taking a wide variety of prey including crustaceans, cephalopods, and reef fishes. At birth, newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a remarkably small beginning that reflects the pelagic spawning strategy common among carangids. Under typical thermal conditions of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], these fertilised eggs hatch after a developmental period lasting about 4.2 days [ab = about 4.2 days], a relatively brief incubation phase that is consistent with the high metabolic demands of tropical marine teleosts. This rapid onset of exogenous feeding is critical for survival during the planktonic larval phase, when predation pressure and starvation risk are both extremely elevated.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Caranx ignobilis is marked by the attainment of a total length of approximately 60 centimeters [Lp = approximately 60 centimeters], which corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the ability to participate in spawning aggregations. During the spawning season, which in many regions coincides with warmer months, a single gravid female can release approximately 230,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 230,000 eggs per spawning event], a value consistent with the high fecundity typical of pelagic spawners. Field observations indicate that females spawn approximately 80 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 80 times per year], yielding a substantial total annual egg production per individual.

The maximum published wet weight recorded for Caranx ignobilis is an impressive 80,000 grams [Wwi = 80,000 grams], a size that places this species among the heaviest of the Carangidae family and underscores its ecological role as a dominant piscivore. Life history theory would predict that such a large-bodied, slow-growing species should exhibit a relatively extended maximum longevity, and indeed, mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing analyses consistently report that the oldest documented individuals reach an age of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] when reared under stable environmental conditions at 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. This lifespan is noteworthy among tropical carangids and allows for multiple decades of reproductive output, contributing to population stability despite potentially high mortality during the early pelagic larval stages.

Juvenile Caranx ignobilis recruit to shallow, structured habitats such as seagrass beds and mangrove fringes, where they benefit from reduced predation pressure and abundant small prey. During this critical post-settlement phase, growth is rapid and individuals quickly increase in both length and mass. The embryonic period, at the species' typical ambient temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], lasts precisely 4.2 days [ab = 4.2 days], a brief developmental duration that is characteristic of tropical marine teleosts with pelagic eggs, where rapid development is an adaptation to reduce vulnerability to planktonic predators. After yolk-sac resorption and the onset of first exogenous feeding, larvae must locate and capture suitable microzooplankton prey within a narrow window to avoid starvation, a bottleneck that governs early cohort survival.

From a broader comparative perspective, the life-history strategy of Caranx ignobilis reflects a classic k-selected pattern among apex marine predators, characterised by late maturity, high fecundity, and a long reproductive lifespan. While the onset of reproductive maturity is conventionally related to the attainment of 60 centimeters [Lp = 60 centimeters] in total length, some studies suggest that earlier maturation may occur at smaller sizes in regions with high fishing pressure. The maximum recorded adult body mass of 80,000 grams [Wwi = 80,000 grams] has been documented from recreational fisheries in the Hawaiian archipelago, supporting the species' reputation as a trophy game fish. A comparative analysis across the Caranx genus reveals that this ultimate wet weight (80,000 grams) [Wwi = 80,000 grams] is among the highest recorded, underscoring the gigantism achievable within the genus when ecological conditions permit extended somatic growth and reduced natural mortality.
